content.text: Angular's default view encapsulation stops a component's styles from leaking out, but it doesn't stop the page's styles from getting in: global stylesheets, inherited properties like
, and CSS custom properties all reach inside. And
isn't the normal way to style a child: Angular strongly discourages it, and it turns your rule into a global one. Give reusable components a styling API instead.

A designer files a bug: the grey "New" badges in the product sidebar turn crimson, but only while the promotions carousel is on screen. Nobody touched the sidebar. The cause is one rule in the carousel's stylesheet,

, written to recolor the single badge inside the carousel. Its author believed component styles are sealed, so the rule could only reach that child. The same bug report adds that the badge text uses the wrong font everywhere, which comes from a
that nobody thought could get in either.
The belief: every Angular component is a sealed box. Its styles can't get out, outside styles can't get in, and when a parent really needs to style something inside a child,
is the standard tool for crossing the wall.
It's half right, which is why it sticks. Angular's docs do say a component's styles don't leak out and affect other components, and you can see it work: write
in its neighbor stays black. Try styling a child's inner
from the parent and nothing happens either, which feels like proof that the wall goes both ways. Then a search for "style child component Angular" turns up years of answers that recommend
, so it looks like the sanctioned escape hatch.
, builds no wall at all. Angular generates a unique attribute, adds it to every element in the component's template, and appends it to every selector in the component's styles:
The rewritten rule can only match elements that carry the attribute, and only the component's own template has it. That's the whole mechanism, and it works in one direction. It controls what
selectors can match. It does nothing to selectors written elsewhere.
has no attribute in it, so it matches every
on the page, including the ones inside your components. The styling guide says it plainly: global styles may still affect elements inside a component with emulated encapsulation.
Inheritance doesn't stop either. In emulated mode the component's elements are ordinary children in the page's DOM, so inherited properties like
flow down from whatever wraps them, and so do
. Stylesheets a component pulls in through a

are treated as external and aren't scoped at all. And when an outside rule and a component rule collide, Angular doesn't promise that the component wins; the guide notes it assumes both have the same specificity.
A parent's rewritten selectors match elements in the parent's template, and the child's host element,
, is one of them. So the parent can style the host: its margin, its width, its custom properties. The
inside belongs to the child's template and carries the child's attribute, so the parent's selectors can't match it. Projected content follows the same rule: elements passed through
are styled by the component that wrote them, not by the one that displays them.

and keeps it only for backwards compatibility.

The better tool is the one the host-elements guide describes: CSS custom properties. The child reads a property with a default, and the parent sets it on the child's host element. Custom properties inherit, so the value reaches the
, and the child decides exactly which parts are configurable.

If you need a stronger boundary,
renders the component into a real shadow root, so its styles can't affect anything outside it. Only the experimental
mode also guarantees that global styles can't affect the elements inside. Both change more than styling: Shadow DOM affects event propagation,
behavior and what DevTools shows, so treat them as an architectural choice, not a CSS fix.
goes the other way and makes all of a component's styles global.

attribute. If it doesn't carry your component's attribute, it isn't in your template, so your component's styles can't match it, whatever the selector says.
A component's styles are added to the page when it renders, and by default Angular removes them again once the component is destroyed. A global
rule therefore breaks other screens only while its component is on screen, which makes the bug look random and hard to reproduce.

When a style looks wrong, open the Computed pane in DevTools, find the property and follow it to the rule that set it. It shows whether it came from your component, a global file or inheritance.

items.text: Emulated encapsulation rewrites your selectors so they can't match outside your template; it doesn't block anything.
Global stylesheets, inherited properties and custom properties still reach inside every component.
A parent can style its child's host element and set custom properties on it, but not the child's inner elements.
is strongly discouraged and turns a rule global; prefer a custom-property styling API.
